messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Librarian
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol Alvarez was seventy-eight, a married librarian who had spent most of her adult life in the United States, but the frightening event she still returned to in her mind belonged to the years when she and her husband were fleeing as refugees from Latin America. She described the escape as a time of sudden, unfinished moments: rushing with only what they could carry, trying to stay quiet, moving from one uncertain place to another, and living with the fear that being seen or stopped could destroy everything. What stayed with her most sharply was not a single complete story she could lay out from beginning to end, but fragments that would arrive with force and without warning. When she tried to speak about it now, she often stopped short, saying that she could not quite put it into words, only that “it was terror, and then more terror.” The memory remained tied to details that made the past feel immediate again. Sometimes, as she thought about those days, she would suddenly smell things she had smelled then, and the return of that odor would make her feel as if she were back in that narrow, exposed passage of time, with her body braced for what might happen next. When the memory came, she felt an intense guilt that sat heavily over it, and she repeatedly blamed herself, turning the event over and over in an effort to understand why it had happened to her and whether she had missed some way to prevent it.

In the years that followed, Marisol built a life that was orderly and careful on the surface. She became a librarian, a role that suited her love of books, quiet, and structure, and it gave her days a predictable rhythm. Yet even in the library, her world had become smaller and more guarded than it once was. She worked hard at keeping busy with other things, filling her time with tasks, shelving, cataloging, and small routines at home with her husband, because idle moments gave room for the memories to come back. She found herself watching the world around her with unusual caution, always scanning for signs that something was not right. Being superalert or on guard had become almost automatic for her, whether she was walking into the library in the morning, standing near the entrance, or sitting in a public place where she could not easily see who was coming and going. Crowded or unfamiliar places felt especially unsafe, and she had come to believe that there were only a very limited number of places where she could truly relax. At home, in a familiar chair and in rooms she knew well, she could settle more fully, but elsewhere she remained tense, measuring exits and noticing movement around her.

Her concentration had also become unreliable in ways that were especially frustrating to her. In the library, where she once took pride in her attention to detail, she now found herself reading the same line again because her mind had drifted back to the past or ahead to what might go wrong. She would lose track in the middle of a task and then feel embarrassed, as if a part of her remained elsewhere. Over time, these lapses made her more self-conscious at work and less comfortable in situations that demanded sustained focus. She did not describe dramatic outbursts or physical panic so much as a persistent inner vigilance, a kind of watchfulness that left her exhausted by the end of the day.

The memories were most unsettling because they arrived without order. She could not tell the story smoothly, and that inability itself distressed her, as though the experience had been too chaotic to hold in language. When the smells came back, or when a place felt too exposed, she would become still and inwardly preoccupied, trying to make sense of what had happened and why she had survived when others had suffered so much. Her guilt intensified each time she remembered, and she often wondered whether she should have done more, moved faster, or somehow protected those she loved better. Those thoughts returned despite her efforts to set them aside.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was still functioning in many respects, but she was tired of living as though danger might be waiting just beyond the familiar places she allowed herself to trust. She came because the constant watchfulness and the repeated turning over of the past had become harder to carry, and because she wanted some relief from the guilt that surfaced whenever the memory intruded. What she feared most was that the past would keep narrowing her life, keeping her confined to only a few safe places and to the same painful questions. What she hoped for, more quietly, was to be able to remember without being overwhelmed by smell, guilt, and the sense that she was back there again.
